source.title: On the Effectiveness of Regularization Against Membership Inference Attacks
source.authors: Yiğitcan Kaya; Sanghyun Hong; Tudor Dumitras

record.tranche_reason: The study reports that label smoothing can reduce the generalization gap while increasing one membership-inference attack's success, and argues that the link between the gap and attack vulnerability is not clear. It does not test the listed claim versions directly.
record.gate_note: The study evaluates regularization against membership-inference attacks and reports validation accuracy, but it does not report training-versus-test error results for the claim versions. It also reports training/test distance-to-confident (DtC) differences, a different measure from the versions' generalization-gap measures.
record.test_reason: The study tests V6 in VGG-style CNNs by comparing validation accuracy with and without dropout across three image datasets. Training-versus-test error gaps are unnecessary for this comparison. These relevant results are missing from the record; the recorded membership-inference and DtC results test none of the versions.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate. The authors conclude that some regularizers mitigate known membership-inference attacks, whereas label smoothing can improve generalization while worsening one attack. Persistent DtC differences suggest possible vulnerability to future attacks, rather than demonstrating such an attack. They also emphasize the value of stronger differential-privacy guarantees.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates regularization mechanisms and membership-inference attacks, not the listed generalization interventions or measures.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset complexity, regularization mechanism and intensity, utility scenario, and attack method affect the reported outcomes.

fits_no_version.finding: Label smoothing can improve generalization while increasing Salem attack advantage, reaching a 58.7% relative increase on CIFAR-100.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Improved generalization does not necessarily reduce vulnerability to every membership-inference attack.

fits_no_version.finding: Training and test samples retain different DtC scores in some settings where existing membership-inference attacks have little or no advantage.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Low success of existing membership-inference attacks does not establish that training and test samples are indistinguishable.

record.problems: The DtC gap is a proxy rather than training-versus-test error. The study does not test the specific conditions in the listed versions.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its coexistence with natural-label generalization.
Width sweeps beyond the width needed to interpolate.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under different tuning budgets.
Batch-size comparisons and adaptations of the training recipe.
Fully connected classifiers, very small training sets, direct evidence of underfitting, and removing dropout and weight decay together under augmentation.
Magnitude-aware weight sharpness and its ranking of generalization gaps.
Removing examples selected by memorization influence and retraining.

missing.what: Standard-dropout validation-accuracy comparisons for each dataset and utility scenario, including dropout probability, baseline accuracy, and relative accuracy change. These directly test V6 and contradict the record's claim that no relevant results were omitted.
missing.locator: Table 2 baselines; Tables 3–5, dropout p rows; Section 3 validation-accuracy and RAD definitions

missing.what: Spatial-dropout validation-accuracy comparisons, recorded separately from standard dropout with their q settings and utility scenarios.

Accuracy comparisons for adding standard or spatial dropout to random cropping on CIFAR-100. Record cropping alone as the intervention baseline and preserve the privacy-based hyperparameter selection.
missing.locator: Section 5; Table 6, c=16 column, rows 5, p and q

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for V6. Reported accuracy changes are relative percentages, not percentage-point changes. Experiments were repeated, but the tables give no uncertainty estimates, so the small accuracy improvements should be read cautiously. Privacy-selected configurations are distinct from maximum-accuracy configurations.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out performance on natural labels.
Width sweeps beyond interpolation and resulting test error.
Adaptive optimizer versus SGD held-out performance.
Whether dropout lowers held-out error; the study reports accuracy changes but does not compare training and test error or establish lower test error.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its ranking of generalization gaps.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the resulting test-accuracy change.

rows.note: DtC difference is not training-versus-test error.
rows.check: DtC measures input perturbations to confident predictions, not any version's outcome. The baseline retains the default L2 weight decay of 1e-6 despite being described as unregularized.

rows.subject: CNNs trained with label smoothing
rows.size_stated: 4-layer, 7-layer, and 9-layer CNNs for Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100, respectively
rows.operation_detail: Applied label smoothing and compared generalization gap and membership-inference success with the standard model.
rows.measure: The authors state that label smoothing reduces the generalization gap but can increase Salem et al.'s attack advantage; on CIFAR-100 the increase is up to 59% in the maximum-accuracy scenario.
rows.note: This result concerns the gap and attack vulnerability, not the claim versions' specified outcomes.
rows.check: Label smoothing's effects on membership inference and generalization do not test a listed version; partial is therefore inappropriate.

rows.subject: CNNs trained with distillation
rows.size_stated: 4-layer, 7-layer, and 9-layer CNNs for Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100, respectively
rows.operation_detail: Measured training/test DtC gap for models trained with distillation.
rows.measure: The text reports 5% Yeom attack advantage and 22% DtC gap.
rows.note: DtC gap is not training-versus-test error; the authors describe it as a stability gap here.
rows.check: Distillation's DtC gap and attack advantage do not measure a listed version.

rows.subject: CNNs trained with regularization
rows.size_stated: 4-layer, 7-layer, and 9-layer CNNs for Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100, respectively
rows.operation_detail: Compared training/test DtC gap with membership-inference success across regularization mechanisms.
rows.measure: The authors state that DtC gaps align well with attack success for these mechanisms.
rows.note: The reported DtC gap is not a training-versus-test error gap.
rows.check: Including dropout as a condition does not make a DtC-versus-attack comparison evidence about dropout lowering held-out error.
